turns.text: I still think about the day I returned to campus after my wife’s surgery. I’d heard rumors that my name had been shouted in front of thousands, but I didn’t expect the violence that met me. Students—some I’d taught, some I’d argued with—dragged me onto a stage, accusing me of persecuting Mao Zedong’s daughter. The truth was, we argued constantly, yes, but it was about ideas. I never imagined those arguments would be twisted into an accusation that nearly cost me my life. What I can’t resolve, even now, is how quickly people I’d known for years turned on me, how a professional disagreement became a crime. That moment—standing on that stage, looking into the eyes of people who wanted me destroyed—still haunts me.

When I think back, what unsettles me most is the collapse of everything I’d taken for granted about daily life—order, dignity, even basic safety. I remember returning to Beijing from the countryside, exhausted, only to find the city transformed. At my institute, research work stopped overnight. Each morning, instead of experiments or discussions, we were herded into rooms to read big-character posters, sometimes until our eyes ached. The air always smelled of ink and sweat, and the walls were layered with paper, each new accusation pasted over the last.

Outside, the city itself felt hostile. I watched my elderly mother—her back bent, face lined—forced to leave for Hebei, her only crime being her family background. On the bus, I saw a Red Guard block a young man from giving his seat to an old woman until she’d recited her class status. The humiliation was everywhere, inescapable. In my own courtyard, things were quieter, but I’d walk past other compounds and see people—sometimes women with old shoes around their necks, sometimes men with signs hung from their shoulders—being paraded and screamed at. I felt powerless, unable to help, unable even to explain to my children why the world had turned upside down. That sense of helplessness—of watching cruelty become ordinary, of seeing children mimic violence—still unsettles me.

RedGuard: The memory that claws at me is the hospital action. We moved in quickly, sealing the gates, lists in hand. The insiders—young staff in red armbands—led us straight to the targets: director, vice directors, a so-called rightist, suspected spies. I remember the tension in the entrance hall, the echo of our boots on the tile, the way the accused lowered their heads as we hung black placards around their necks. The director tried to resist, shouting that we were making a mistake, but his voice was drowned out by slogans. 

We marched them through the streets, a cart behind us loaded with books and Western clothes. At the main intersection, the bonfire was already roaring. We tossed their possessions in—photographs curling in the heat, a silk scarf catching flame—and forced them to stand in front of the fire, sweat pouring down their faces, ash settling on their hair. I remember the nurse, the one accused of being an American spy. She said nothing, just stared at the ground. That night, she hanged herself in the duty room. We found her too late. Even now, I can still see the mark on her neck, the way her body looked in the fluorescent light. 

What I can’t reconcile is how quickly we went from chanting slogans to watching someone die. I believed we were making revolution, but sometimes I wonder what was really driving us. Was it belief, or something darker?

I remember the sunlight on the stone steps outside our building. Most days, I sat there with my little brother and sister, peeling sunflower seeds, listening to the distant shouting that sometimes drifted over the compound wall. Inside, our world felt safe—rows of neat barracks, the smell of rice cooking, the tap-tap of slippers in the hallway. 

School had stopped, so we spent hours making things from scraps: paper windmills, little boats for the lake, cricket cages from old matchboxes. Sometimes we’d hear loudspeakers blaring outside, or see lines of people marching past on the avenue, but to me it was just noise—something grownups cared about. 

What I never understood, and still can’t quite grasp, is how so much pain was happening just beyond our gates while my days felt so easy. I didn’t know anyone who disappeared. I didn’t see anyone beaten or paraded. My father never spoke about the meetings he went to, and my mother kept us busy with chores and games. I thought the world was mostly kind. When I hear what others lived through, I wonder why our compound felt like an island. Maybe we were protected because of the uniforms, or maybe the adults just hid things well. I still can’t decide if I was lucky, or just blind.

CRBeneficiary: My memory is a single object: the Peking University badge. Before that, every day was hunger and calculation — how to stretch a handful of cornmeal, how to avoid the shame of begging for extra soup in the canteen. My world was small: a mud house, ten mouths, the sound of my mother slicing a pumpkin into pieces so thin you could see light through them. I studied because it was the only thing I could control, but by the time the Cultural Revolution began, that pathway was torn away. 

School stopped meaning anything. I saw teachers forced to kneel in the mud, their glasses smashed, their dignity stripped by students who used to hide from them in the halls. I learned to keep my head down, to watch the slogans on the walls change week by week. The only ladder left was the army. I joined, not out of belief but because it was the only way off the land. I scrubbed latrines, carried loads until my hands bled, and tried to make myself useful — not out of loyalty, but because I knew what happened to people who stood out for the wrong reasons.

Then, out of nowhere, I was told I’d been recommended to Peking University. No exam, no explanation. Just a form, an order, a train ticket. When I held that badge in my hand, I realized how little my own effort mattered compared to the tides of the time. I didn’t even know what ‘Hindi’ was — I thought maybe it was a kind of revolution, or a code word for something secret. But it didn’t matter. That badge meant I had crossed a line no one in my village had ever crossed. I still can’t decide if I deserved it, or if I was just lucky that the system needed someone like me at that moment. And I never stopped thinking about everyone left behind — the ones who studied just as hard, but whose names were never called.

Moderator: All five recollections are consistent with historical evidence about the Cultural Revolution’s upheaval, including public denunciations, the abrupt halt to research and education, the Red Guard’s violent campaigns, the relative insulation of military families, and the new university admission policies that prioritized political background over academic exams. RedGuard’s mention of suicides among accused “class enemies” is sadly accurate, as such tragedies occurred in many institutions. CRBeneficiary’s story reflects the “worker-peasant-soldier” recommendation system, which replaced entrance exams and gave rural and military youth unprecedented access to elite universities, often at the expense of traditional meritocracy. The sense of randomness and survivor’s guilt described is echoed in many memoirs from this era.

RedGuard, you say you believed you were making revolution, but you describe actions that destroyed lives and ended in death. Did you ever stop to question the slogans you were shouting, or wonder if Mao Zedong himself would have approved of the violence you were unleashing? I argued with his daughter about ideas—never about her background, never about her loyalty—and for that I was nearly killed. You talk about belief, but all I saw from the Red Guards was a hunger for power and purity, with no room for doubt or mercy. When you saw the nurse’s body, did you feel any responsibility, or did you just move on to the next target?

I want to say something to both of you, Professor and RedGuard. I saw people like you, Professor, paraded through university squares, heads pushed down, faces covered in ink, signs hanging from your necks. I saw people like you, RedGuard, standing on chairs, bellowing slogans, faces red with excitement or rage, sometimes trembling with something I couldn’t name. I watched as crowds—sometimes hundreds, sometimes just a handful—waited for the next accusation, the next confession, the next humiliation.

What I still can’t accept is how quickly the line between “revolution” and cruelty dissolved. I watched old comrades—men and women who had survived wars, who had given everything to the Party—forced to kneel for hours, spat on by children. I stood at the back of those meetings, feeling sick, unable to intervene, knowing that any protest would only make things worse for me and my family. 

I never understood why those at the top, especially Chairman Mao, allowed this to happen. I saw the posters praising him, the chants, the portraits everywhere, but I never saw any real protection for those who had sacrificed for the country. Did he not see what was happening? Or did he believe that humiliation and violence were necessary for some greater purpose?

I sometimes wonder, RedGuard, what you felt when you looked into the eyes of the people you denounced. Did you see them as enemies, or did you ever recognize their humanity? And for those of us who watched from the sidelines, what could we have done? I still don’t know if silence was cowardice or simply survival.

RedGuard: Professor, I remember the first time I led a house search—how my hands shook when I pulled open drawers, how the old woman whose home we ransacked just sat there, silent, not even crying. I told myself over and over that it was for the revolution, for Mao. We read his words every morning, and the slogans felt like armor. But the truth is, most of us never saw Mao, never heard him speak except through the radio or through loudspeakers. His portrait watched over us, but he was distant, almost mythic. We convinced ourselves he would approve, because every order came stamped with his name.

When I saw the nurse’s body, I didn’t feel relief or triumph. I felt cold. I remember standing in the hallway, the white tiles under my feet, the fluorescent light flickering, and thinking: this isn’t what I imagined revolution would feel like. But I didn’t stop. I told myself she must have been guilty, that weakness was a sign of hidden guilt. That’s what we were taught—struggle against yourself, struggle against others. I felt responsible, yes, but I also felt trapped. If I had hesitated, I would have become the next target. I saw it happen to others—one day you’re leading the struggle, the next day you’re the one with a placard around your neck.

To Researcher, I’ll say this: when you’re in the crowd, shouting, it’s easy to lose sight of individuals. The slogans fill your head, the group pulls you along. I looked into people’s eyes, but I also looked away. Sometimes I saw terror, sometimes I saw contempt. Some people spat at us, some begged. But I rarely saw anything that made me stop. I was young, angry, and afraid of being left behind. If you stood by in silence, maybe you survived, but I wonder—did you ever feel the urge to shout back, or did you bury it so deep that you can’t find it anymore?

I never saw any of this up close—the parades, the shouting, the violence. I only glimpsed the world outside our gates when I followed my mother to the market, and even then, she’d hurry us past any crowds, pulling us away if we lingered. The only time I remember being truly frightened was when a group of older youths in red armbands marched past the compound, banging on doors and shouting slogans. My little brother started to cry, and my mother scooped him up and told us to stay inside, away from the windows.

Inside, life felt normal—almost peaceful. But now, hearing your stories, I wonder what my parents were protecting us from. I remember the way my father’s face changed when the loudspeakers started up. He’d close the window, turn up the radio with music, and tell us to play quietly. I never saw him wear his uniform around the house, only when he left for meetings. I thought he was just being careful, but now I think he was hiding his fear.

I can’t imagine what it felt like to be in those crowds, shouting or being shouted at. I didn’t know anyone who was denounced, but I wonder now—if I had, would I have believed the slogans? Would I have joined in? At the time, I thought Mao Zedong was like a god—his portrait was everywhere, even in our little classroom before school stopped. Did any of you actually believe in him, deep down? Or did you just pretend, because it was safer?

CRBeneficiary: I never saw a portrait of Mao Zedong that wasn’t faded or peeling at the corners. In my village, he was a face on a poster above the commune office, a name in red ink on the loudspeakers. We didn’t have the luxury of belief — we had hunger. When the slogans changed, we repeated them, because not repeating them meant trouble. I remember one winter, chopping sweet potato vines for feed, hearing the older boys in the production team argue about whether the new line was true revolution or just another way to sort the lucky from the unlucky. Most of us kept quiet and worked faster.

When I got to the army, the discipline was different, but the rituals were the same. We read the Little Red Book every morning, recited lines until our mouths were dry, but nobody I knew talked about Mao as if he was a real person. He was a test you had to pass every day, not a leader you could touch. I saw people denounced for saying the wrong thing, or for not saying enough. In the army, I watched a young man get sent away for laughing at the wrong time during a study session. That’s when I understood: belief wasn’t the point — survival was.

Later, at Peking University, I saw how the badge changed everything. Suddenly, my background was valuable, and people wanted to hear about my loyalty, my hardship. But I never felt loyal — I felt watched. I didn’t trust the slogans, but I learned to say them louder than anyone else, because I knew what happened to people who fell silent. You ask if I believed in Mao. I believed in not starving. I believed in not being sent back to the fields. That was my ideology. 

Do any of you think the slogans ever meant the same thing to people in the city as to people in the countryside? Or was it always just a kind of mask, worn for safety, no matter where you stood?

Moderator: All participants’ memories accurately reflect the diversity of experience during the Cultural Revolution. ProfessorR and Researcher’s accounts show the real dangers of intellectual life and the unpredictable violence faced by “class enemies.” RedGuard’s description of being caught between belief, fear, and conformity is consistent with documented Red Guard testimonies. CRTeenFromBeijing’s sense of isolation within a military compound matches the relative protection afforded to some military families, though not all were immune from political campaigns. CRBeneficiary’s observation that survival, rather than belief, drove behavior in rural areas is supported by oral histories; for many, political ritual was a means of self-preservation rather than genuine faith. The mask of slogans often concealed private doubts in both city and countryside, though the stakes and forms of pressure could differ.
